factProposals.value: City staff are users with roles: system administrator, supervisor, field crew, clerk, planner and auditor (placeholder roles until the city confirms its own). Outside systems remain separate API clients.
Each person uses a personal key that is shown once and stored only as a hash. Their permissions come from their current roles on every request, and access checks fail closed.

Only a system administrator, acting with their own key, can add users, grant or remove roles, and issue or revoke keys. A workflow step can require a role, for example only a supervisor signs off a repair.
Every audit entry made in a person's request records their verified user id, alongside readable actor text. Refused access attempts, including acting under someone else's name, are audited.
Auditors can read the audit trail filtered by user, item, action and time range, a page at a time; reading it is itself audited.
The city's real staff roles and permissions, and whether staff must sign in through the city's own identity system, are not known.

decisions.statement: Use personal API keys for people instead of passwords or single sign-on.
decisions.rationale: No access to the city's identity system; keys reuse the hashed-key design already in place and can sit behind single sign-on later.

decisions.statement: Make role permissions the same names as API client scopes.
decisions.rationale: Every existing endpoint enforces people's roles without changes of its own.

decisions.statement: Take the acting user from the key and refuse an actor name that differs.
decisions.rationale: Before, the audit trail held whatever name a caller typed; now it can show who really acted.

decisions.statement: Refuse access changes made with an outside system's key, even with access:admin.
decisions.rationale: Every access change must have a verified user id.

decisions.statement: Never let the last active system administrator lose the role; create the first one with a one-off command that refuses if one exists.
decisions.rationale: The city must never be locked out of managing access, and the setup command must not allow taking over a running system.

limitations.statement: The six built-in roles are placeholders, and administrators cannot define new roles yet.
Users cannot yet be edited or deactivated through the API; that is user management, still to come.
There is no password or single sign-on login; people use personal keys.
Audit entries made before this change, and entries from outside systems, have no verified user id.
Auditors see full before and after values in the audit trail, including work order details.
